name: Snipe
question: What is creating the early move?
intro: Read the engine behind the first move: liquidity, buyers, sellers, and the supply changing hands.

lessons.title: Price moves at the margin
lessons.question: Did capital grow, or did the last price change?
lessons.definition: The next trade changes the price available to the trade after it. In an AMM pool, reserves and liquidity shape that price.
lessons.why: A small trade can change the displayed valuation of the whole supply.
checks: Exact pool and current liquidity
Trade size relative to pool depth
Market cap change versus observed trade value
lessons.healthy: Price changes are read alongside pool depth and surrounding trades.
lessons.dangerous: A market-cap jump is treated as the same amount of new capital.
lessons.takeaway: A new price can revalue the whole supply.
example: A token has 1 million circulating units at $0.10.
The displayed price rises to $0.12: market cap rises from $100k to $120k.
That $20k change does not tell you how much was traded.
evidence: Choose an exact contract. Compare estimated MC tiers with observed swap value; these are different measures.
lessons.deeper: The original outline uses an auction analogy. Many meme pools use automated pricing instead of an order book. The useful shared idea is marginal pricing, not a literal match between named buyers and sellers.

lessons.title: Liquidity & price impact
lessons.question: How much does this order disturb the pool?
lessons.definition: Price impact is the change in execution price caused by your order relative to available liquidity.
lessons.why: The same dollar order can produce very different fills in different pools.
checks: Current executable quote for the intended size
Pool depth and route
Impact, fees, and slippage tolerance separately
lessons.healthy: The order fits the quote and the expected cost is understood.
lessons.dangerous: Thin depth or broad tolerance turns a modest order into a poor fill.
lessons.mistake: Expecting equal buy sizes to create equal moves.
example: Compare a $1k order in a deep pool and a thin pool.
The thin pool may offer a much worse average execution price.
Compare the actual quotes, not just the chart prices.
evidence: Check reported liquidity as context. Obtain current impact and execution quotes externally.
lessons.deeper: Price sensitivity is not automatically strength: it can amplify selling too. A ratio of price change to sampled net buying is descriptive, not a stable capital-efficiency score. Liquidity, routes, and missing trades can all change the comparison.

lessons.title: Buy/sell pressure
lessons.question: Are the buys actually outweighing the sells?
lessons.definition: Pressure combines trade value, frequency, and how long the activity persists.
lessons.why: Many small buys can be outweighed by one large sell.
checks: Buy and sell value in the same window
Typical sizes and the largest trades
Whether the pattern persists in the next window
lessons.healthy: Buying persists and repeated selling meets new demand.
lessons.dangerous: Green transaction counts hide large sell value.
lessons.mistake: Counting colors instead of measuring value.
lessons.takeaway: Read size, frequency, and persistence together.
example: 20 buys × $100 = $2,000 bought.
This sample has 19 more buys, but $3,000 more sell value.
evidence: Compare buy/sell value and swap sizes for one listing and time window. Net value describes the returned sample.
lessons.deeper: Size × frequency × persistence is a thinking aid, not a defined trading score. Observed buy value minus sell value is not a measurement of total capital entering the token, and it does not by itself determine the price outcome.

lessons.title: Supply transfer
lessons.question: Whose inventory is changing hands?
lessons.definition: Supply transfer moves inventory from early holders to later buyers.
lessons.why: Remaining low-cost inventory can become future sell pressure.
checks: Early-wallet balances before and after sales
Transfers versus executed sells
Remaining inventory relative to liquidity
lessons.healthy: Actual sales and new ownership can be traced.
lessons.dangerous: Transfers to related wallets disguise continuing control.
lessons.mistake: Assuming lower concentration proves independent ownership.
lessons.takeaway: Track what remains, not just what moved.
example: An early wallet holds 8% of supply.
It transfers 5% to fresh addresses and still holds 3%.
The visible balance fell; common control may not have changed.
lessons.external: Use an explorer and wallet history to trace transfers, trades, and related balances. Meme Fast does not establish common ownership.
lessons.deeper: Sellable supply is a hypothesis about inventory that may be offered, not an observable list of everyone willing to sell. Holder turnover needs transaction history; a snapshot alone cannot establish it.

lessons.title: Early wallet flow
lessons.question: Who is behind the buying?
lessons.definition: Wallet flow asks whether a participant is buying, holding, transferring, or selling over time.
lessons.why: The same trade value can come from independent buyers or one coordinated operator.
checks: Wallet history and remaining exposure
Funding links and transfers
Observed entry cost and prior sales
lessons.healthy: Attribution and behavior are supported by traceable history.
lessons.dangerous: A reputation label or many addresses substitutes for evidence.
lessons.mistake: Treating every buy as equally informative.
lessons.takeaway: Investigate the source of the flow.
example: Ten addresses each buy $500.
All ten were funded through the same small wallet moments earlier.
That is a coordination lead, not ten proven independent buyers.
evidence: Use transaction senders as leads, then trace them externally. Routers can appear as senders; wallet identity and cost basis are not verified here.
lessons.deeper: A transaction bundle groups transactions; a wallet cluster is an inference about related addresses. Neither automatically proves malicious intent. Shared exchange funding, routers, and incomplete trade history can mislead attribution.

lessons.title: Momentum & acceleration
lessons.question: Is the activity strengthening or just staying busy?
lessons.definition: Momentum is sustained directional activity. Acceleration is a change in its pace or strength.
lessons.why: A busy token can be slowing down while its chart still looks strong.
checks: Comparable, separate time windows
Trade value, size, and frequency together
Liquidity changes and missing observations
lessons.healthy: Several comparable observations show demand strengthening.
lessons.dangerous: One spike or overlapping totals is called acceleration.
lessons.mistake: Waiting for a giant candle, then assuming the engine is still strengthening.
lessons.takeaway: Compare the pace, not just the total.
example: Two separate five-minute windows show 10 buys, then 20.
Buy value rises too, while liquidity stays similar.
That supports rising activity; it does not predict the next candle.
evidence: Review sampled 5m activity and freshness, then compare actual windows in Inspect. Nested 5m/1h/24h totals are not separate periods.
lessons.deeper: More trades can mean automated churn. Higher buy share can coexist with falling total value. Demand, liquidity, and price response need to be compared together before describing acceleration.

lessons.title: Attention → capital
lessons.question: Did the story bring buyers, or only posts?
lessons.definition: Attention becomes market evidence when discussion is accompanied by observable trading activity.
lessons.why: A mention count alone does not establish demand or explain its source.
checks: Source and exact token association
Attention and flow in comparable periods
Whether activity continues after the initial mention
lessons.healthy: Source evidence and market activity support the same research question.
lessons.dangerous: Repeated posts are treated as proof of independent buying.
lessons.mistake: Equating social activity with capital inflow.
lessons.takeaway: Compare attention with activity; keep causation open.
example: Indexed mentions rise after a headline.
Observed buy value stays flat in the comparable period.
Attention increased; buying conversion is not demonstrated.
evidence: Open source evidence, confirm the contract, then compare flow in Inspect. RSS counts do not measure total engagement or unique buyers.
lessons.deeper: Even when posts and buying rise together, that does not prove the posts caused the buys. Indexed RSS can lag, and the original exposure → interest → visit → buy loop is a conceptual path, not measured conversion analytics.

lessons.title: Push, Hold or Fail
lessons.question: What happened after the first push?
lessons.definition: Push describes expansion; Hold describes a pause that retains the range; Fail describes loss of that range.
lessons.why: The pause helps test whether buyers are still meeting supply.
checks: Price range before and after the pause
Repeated selling and subsequent recovery
Liquidity, coverage, and alternative explanations
lessons.healthy: The range holds through repeated selling and buying resumes.
lessons.dangerous: Rebounds weaken while the range and liquidity deteriorate.
lessons.takeaway: Read the pause. Leave missing evidence unknown.
example: Price pushes higher, then pauses in a new range.
Several sells occur and price repeatedly recovers within it.
Hold is a working description; another Push still needs new evidence.
evidence: Compare candle ranges and observed swaps. Push/Hold/Fail are lesson interpretations, not automated Meme Fast classifications.
lessons.deeper: Push → Hold → Push and Push → distribution → Fail are possible paths, not rules. When history, liquidity, or wallet evidence is insufficient, use Unknown rather than forcing a state.
